Cannabis and Pets: Can CBD Help Your Dog or Cat?

By HowToEdibles Editorial Team March 17, 2026 9 min read

Learn about CBD for pets — what the research says, potential benefits for anxiety and pain, proper dosing by weight, THC toxicity risks, and how to choose safe pet CBD products.

Home / Articles / Cannabis and Pets: Can CBD Help Your Dog or Cat?

Short answer

Never give a dog or cat THC. The ASPCA lists marijuana as toxic to both, with signs ranging from vomiting and loss of coordination to seizures and coma. CBD may help some dogs: small trials found less arthritis pain and fewer seizures. But the FDA has not approved any cannabis product for animals, and dogs given CBD in those trials showed rises in a liver enzyme. Use CBD only under a veterinarian's supervision.

Not veterinary advice

This article is general education, not veterinary advice. Talk to your veterinarian before giving your pet any CBD or cannabis product, especially if your pet takes other medications. If your pet may have eaten a cannabis product, call your vet or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center at (888) 426-4435 right away (a consultation fee may apply).

As cannabis has become more mainstream and widely available, pet owners are increasingly curious about whether cannabinoids — particularly CBD — might benefit their furry companions. The pet CBD market has exploded in recent years, with products ranging from tinctures and treats to topical balms marketed for everything from anxiety relief to joint support. But behind the marketing hype lies an important and nuanced conversation about what is safe, what is effective, and what could be genuinely dangerous for your pets.

This guide provides an honest, science-based look at cannabis and pets. We will explore the research behind CBD for dogs and cats, explain why THC poses serious risks to animals, and give you practical guidance on product selection, why dosing belongs with your veterinarian, and when to call for help. Whether you are considering CBD for an aging dog with arthritis or a cat with anxiety, understanding the facts is essential for keeping your pet safe.

The endocannabinoid system in animals

Just like humans, dogs, cats, and virtually all vertebrate animals possess an endocannabinoid system (ECS). This biological system, discovered in the early 1990s, is a complex network of receptors, enzymes, and endogenous cannabinoids that plays a crucial role in regulating a wide range of physiological processes including pain perception, mood, appetite, immune function, and homeostasis. The fact that animals share this system with humans is the foundational reason why cannabinoids can affect them at all.

The ECS in animals contains the same two primary receptor types found in humans: CB1 receptors, which are concentrated in the brain and central nervous system, and CB2 receptors, found primarily in the immune system and peripheral organs. However, there is one critically important difference: dogs appear to be far more sensitive to THC than people. A commonly cited explanation is that dogs have a high density of CB1 receptors in certain brain regions, though this is still being studied. What might produce a mild buzz in a human can cause severe neurological symptoms in a dog.

CBD interacts with the endocannabinoid system differently than THC. Rather than binding directly to CB1 receptors, CBD works indirectly by influencing the ECS to use its own endocannabinoids more effectively and by interacting with other receptor systems including serotonin receptors and vanilloid receptors involved in pain perception. This indirect mechanism is why CBD does not produce intoxication in either humans or animals and is generally considered to have a wider safety margin than THC.

Cats also have an endocannabinoid system, though research on feline responses to cannabinoids is less extensive than canine research. What we do know is that cats appear to metabolize cannabinoids differently than dogs, and they can be particularly sensitive to certain compounds. Cats lack some of the liver enzymes that help process certain substances, which is why they are famously sensitive to medications like aspirin and essential oils. This metabolic difference means that dosing for cats requires extra caution, and any CBD product used should be specifically formulated and tested for feline use.

Potential benefits of CBD for dogs and cats

The most robust research on CBD for pets has focused on dogs, with several well-designed clinical studies producing encouraging results. A 2018 placebo-controlled crossover trial at Cornell University's College of Veterinary Medicine, funded by a CBD company, followed 16 dogs with osteoarthritis. On CBD, owners reported less pain and more activity, and veterinary pain scores improved. Veterinary lameness and weight-bearing scores did not change. Owners reported no side effects, but blood tests showed the liver enzyme alkaline phosphatase (ALP) rising during CBD treatment. The researchers advised monitoring liver enzymes in dogs receiving hemp products.

Epilepsy is another area where CBD has shown particular promise for dogs. A 2019 randomized, blinded trial at Colorado State University added CBD or a placebo to the usual anti-seizure medicine of dogs with hard-to-treat epilepsy. Only 16 dogs were analyzed. Dogs on CBD had a significant median 33% drop in seizure frequency compared with placebo, but the share of dogs whose seizures fell by half or more was similar in both groups. Dogs on CBD also had higher ALP, and two were withdrawn because of ataxia. That makes CBD a possible add-on to conventional treatment that needs larger studies, not a replacement for it. It is worth noting that CBD has already received FDA approval for treating certain forms of epilepsy in humans through the drug Epidiolex.

Anxiety is perhaps the most common reason pet owners reach for CBD products. Dogs can suffer from separation anxiety, noise phobias such as fear of thunderstorms and fireworks, and generalized anxiety. While large-scale clinical trials on CBD for canine anxiety are still limited, anecdotal evidence from veterinarians and pet owners is abundant, and preliminary research suggests that CBD's interaction with serotonin receptors may produce genuine anxiolytic effects. Many pet owners report that their dogs are calmer during stressful events after receiving CBD, though individual responses vary considerably.

For cats, the research is less developed but growing. Anecdotal reports and early studies suggest that CBD may help with feline anxiety, inflammatory conditions, and age-related discomfort. A 2019 Cornell study gave a single dose of a CBD-rich hemp product to 8 healthy dogs and 8 healthy cats. Cats reached much lower blood levels of CBD than dogs, which suggests they absorb or eliminate it differently. Some cats licked excessively and shook their heads during dosing, and one cat had a persistent rise in the liver enzyme ALT. Some veterinarians are cautiously recommending CBD for cats with conditions like inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease-related nausea, and behavioral anxiety, though they emphasize the need for more research and careful product selection.

THC toxicity in pets and warning signs

While CBD appears to be relatively safe for pets, THC is a fundamentally different story. The ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center lists marijuana as toxic to both dogs and cats, and THC is the compound responsible. Accidental exposure is a growing concern as cannabis products become more common in homes. It is absolutely essential that pet owners understand the risks and know how to respond if accidental exposure occurs.

Dogs are particularly vulnerable to THC. Even small amounts of THC that would produce mild effects in a human can cause significant distress in a dog. Common symptoms of THC toxicity in dogs include severe lethargy and drowsiness, loss of coordination and stumbling (ataxia), urinary incontinence, dilated pupils, exaggerated startle response, vomiting, drooling, low heart rate, and hypothermia. In more severe cases, dogs may experience tremors, seizures, or fall into a stupor-like state that can last for many hours. While fatal outcomes are rare, they have been reported, particularly in very small dogs or when edibles containing chocolate or xylitol are involved, as these ingredients carry their own toxicity risks.

Cats are also at risk from THC exposure, though they tend to encounter cannabis products less frequently than dogs simply because they are generally less inclined to eat things indiscriminately. Symptoms of THC toxicity in cats are similar to those in dogs and include extreme lethargy, wobbling, hypersensitivity to touch and sound, dilated pupils, and in some cases, agitation and vocalization. Cats may also drool excessively and refuse food. Because cats metabolize cannabinoids differently, the effects can sometimes take longer to resolve.

If you suspect your pet has ingested a THC product, take action immediately. Contact your veterinarian or the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center (888-426-4435, available 24/7; a consultation fee may apply) right away. Be honest about what your pet consumed — veterinarians are not there to judge, and accurate information is critical for proper treatment. Treatment may include induced vomiting if ingestion was recent, activated charcoal to reduce absorption, IV fluids for hydration and temperature regulation, and monitoring in a quiet, dark environment to minimize sensory stimulation. With prompt supportive care most pets recover, though signs can last many hours and deaths, while uncommon, do occur. The experience is frightening for both pet and owner.

Prevention is always better than treatment. Store all cannabis products — edibles, flower, concentrates, and tinctures — in secure, pet-proof containers kept well out of reach. Cannabis edibles are especially dangerous because they often taste appealing to dogs and may contain chocolate, which is independently toxic to canines. Never leave edibles unattended on counters, tables, or in bags that a curious pet could access. If you use cannabis at home, be mindful of where you place your products and treat them with the same care you would give any medication.

How to choose safe pet CBD products

The FDA has not approved cannabis for any use in animals, and pet CBD products are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness, or quality before sale. That means that product quality varies enormously. Some products contain exactly what they claim, while others may have significantly more or less CBD than labeled, or may contain contaminants including heavy metals, pesticides, or unwanted levels of THC. Choosing a safe, effective product requires careful evaluation, and cutting corners on quality is not worth the risk when your pet's health is at stake.

The most important thing to look for is a certificate of analysis (COA) from an independent, third-party laboratory. A legitimate COA will verify the cannabinoid content, confirming that the product contains the amount of CBD claimed on the label and that THC levels are below the legal limit of 0.3 percent — or ideally, non-detectable. The COA should also test for contaminants including heavy metals like lead and mercury, residual pesticides, residual solvents from the extraction process, and microbial contaminants like mold and bacteria. Reputable companies make their COAs easily accessible on their websites or via QR codes on their packaging.

Choose products specifically formulated for pets rather than repurposing human CBD products. Pet-specific formulations come in smaller, easier-to-measure strengths and typically use carrier oils that are safe for pets, such as MCT oil derived from coconut. Some human CBD products contain ingredients that may be safe for people but harmful to animals — for example, certain essential oils, artificial sweeteners like xylitol (which is extremely toxic to dogs), or flavorings that may not agree with an animal's digestive system. Pet CBD products also come in formats designed for easy administration, such as flavored tinctures, soft chews, and treats.

When evaluating brands, look for companies that are transparent about their sourcing and manufacturing processes. The best pet CBD companies use hemp grown in the United States under regulated conditions, employ clean extraction methods such as CO2 extraction, and follow good manufacturing practices (GMP). Customer reviews and veterinary endorsements can be helpful indicators of quality, though they should not replace your own due diligence. Be wary of companies that make specific medical claims about their products, as this is not permitted under FDA regulations and may indicate a less reputable operation.

Dosing CBD for pets by weight

There is no FDA-approved CBD product for pets and no established, validated dose for dogs or cats. The doses used in published studies were tested in small groups of animals under veterinary monitoring, often with blood work, and they don't translate safely into a do-it-yourself chart. The right amount, if any, depends on your pet's species, weight, age, liver and kidney health, other medications, and the CBD content of the specific product, which often differs from the label. For these reasons we don't publish a dosing table for pets. Please work out a plan with your veterinarian.

If your veterinarian agrees that CBD is worth trying, they will choose a starting amount, tell you how to adjust it, and schedule follow-up. Because studies in dogs found rising liver enzymes, that follow-up may include blood work. You can help by keeping a simple log of each dose, the time you gave it, and any changes you notice in behavior, appetite, energy, coordination, or symptoms, then sharing it at check-ups.

Cats need extra caution. In a 2019 study they reached much lower blood levels of CBD than dogs given a similar dose, which suggests they absorb or eliminate it differently, and some showed licking and head shaking during dosing. Never give a cat a product made for dogs or people. Make sure your veterinarian knows about every medication your pet takes, since CBD can interact with drugs processed by the same liver enzymes. And never give any pet a product containing THC.

What veterinarians say about cannabis for pets

The veterinary community's stance on cannabis for pets has evolved significantly in recent years. While the profession was initially cautious to the point of silence, a growing body of research and increasing client demand have led many veterinarians to engage more openly with the topic. Veterinary organizations have generally called for more research on cannabis in animals.

Some states have passed laws that explicitly allow veterinarians to discuss cannabis products with clients. What veterinarians may legally discuss or recommend still varies by state. These legal protections are important because, prior to such legislation, many veterinarians felt they could not openly discuss cannabis with pet owners without risking their professional licenses. The result was that pet owners were making decisions about cannabis for their pets based on internet advice rather than professional veterinary guidance.

Among veterinarians who are knowledgeable about cannabinoid medicine, the consensus is generally cautiously optimistic about CBD and clearly negative about THC for pets. Most will emphasize that while the early research on CBD for pain, epilepsy, and anxiety in dogs is encouraging, we are still in the relatively early stages of understanding long-term effects, optimal dosing protocols, and potential drug interactions. They typically recommend starting with the lowest effective dose, using only high-quality, lab-tested products, and maintaining regular check-ups including blood work to monitor liver function, since CBD is metabolized through the liver.

What virtually all veterinarians agree on is that THC should never be deliberately given to pets and that preventing accidental exposure is a critical responsibility for cannabis-using pet owners. They also caution against replacing proven veterinary treatments with CBD without professional consultation. CBD may complement conventional treatments, but it should not be viewed as a substitute for established medical therapies, particularly for serious conditions. If you are considering CBD for your pet, the best first step is always a conversation with your veterinarian, who can evaluate your pet's specific health situation and help you make an informed decision.
